segments.title: Opening: The Boy Who Would Become a Man

utterances.text: Welcome to David Copperfield Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's great autobiography of the imagination.
Over the course of this series, we'll be following one of literature's most enduring heroes from his bewildered childhood in Suffolk to the hard-won wisdom of his adult years.
Each episode, we bring together three remarkable readers to unpack the passages, the people, and the ideas that make this novel so inexhaustible.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than practically anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score, in rhythms and rests and comic timing.
Sir Edmund Leigh spent decades at Oxford teaching the novel as moral form — he reads character with the patience and precision of a watchmaker.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen brings the sharp eye of the cultural historian — for him, every institution in a Dickens novel is a machine, and the question is always: who does it crush?
We begin at the beginning — with a boy who is, as the novel's famous first line asks, the hero of his own life.
What strikes me first, every time I come back to this novel, is that it opens with a dare.
Dickens puts the question of heroism directly to the reader before the story has even drawn breath.
And what I love — what makes this novel different from nearly anything else he wrote — is that David himself is never quite sure of the answer.
He is the most uncertain hero in Victorian fiction, and that uncertainty is completely deliberate.
There's a passage I want to get to quite early, because I think it sets the emotional key for everything that follows.
It's the adult David, looking back on the moment he returns home to find Murdstone already installed — and he asks what a single kind word might have done.
Edmund, that passage is yours — but I'll be curious what you make of it.
It is, I think, the moral centre of the first half of the novel — and Dickens places it with extraordinary care.
The adult narrator looking back at his childhood self — that double perspective is what gives the passage its particular anguish.
Let me read it, because the prose really must be heard.
"God help me, I might have been improved for my whole life, I might have been made another creature perhaps, for life, by a kind word at that season."

"A word of encouragement and explanation, of pity for my childish ignorance, of welcome home, of reassurance to me that it was home, might have made me dutiful to him in my heart henceforth, instead of in my hypocritical outside, and might have made me respect instead of hate him."
That word — hypocritical — is absolutely devastating.
The child is not pretending to virtue — he is being forced into the performance of it by an adult who demands compliance without offering love.
Murdstone does not corrupt David — he simply closes the door on a better David that might have been.
Edmund is absolutely right that the passage is devastating — but I'd push on where the blame is located.
Dickens frames this as a question of individual character — Murdstone's failure of imagination, his failure of kindness.
But Murdstone is not an aberration — he is a type, a recognisable Victorian patriarch who believes discipline is love's superior form.
The system rewards men like Murdstone — it gives them legal authority over women and children, property over persons.
And look at what happens to Clara Copperfield in that passage — she watches her son standing scared and strange, and the word is not spoken.
She cannot speak it — not because she doesn't feel it, but because Murdstone has already colonised the domestic space entirely.
That silence is not individual failure — it is the structure of mid-Victorian marriage made visible in a single agonising moment.
I take Daniel's point about the structure of the marriage — it is a real and terrible thing.
But I think Dickens is ultimately more interested in the moral failure of this specific man than in the institution he represents.
The novel is not a programme — it is a portrait, and what makes it endure is precisely that individuality.
Murdstone is not interchangeable with any other Victorian patriarch — he is specifically, meticulously Murdstone: cold, handsome, and entirely without pity.
And yet — and this is what I find so thrilling about the novel's construction — Dickens is equally capable of sheer comic delight in the very next breath.
Because this is not a tragedy — it is a novel, in the great capacious Victorian sense, and it holds grief and comedy in the same hand simultaneously.
Think of Miss Mowcher — the description of her entrance in Chapter twenty-four is one of the great comic set-pieces in English prose.
David is waiting for her to appear in the doorway — and nothing appears.

"There came waddling round a sofa which stood between me and it, a pursy dwarf, of about forty or forty-five, with a very large head and face, a pair of roguish grey eyes, and such extremely little arms, that, to enable herself to lay a finger archly against her snub nose, as she ogled Steerforth, she was obliged to meet the finger half-way, and lay her nose against it."
The nose meets the finger half-way — it is the funniest piece of physical comedy in the novel, and it is entirely written for the voice.
You cannot appreciate that sentence on the page the way you can when you perform it.
Oliver's right that it's brilliantly funny — but I want to notice something about the energy behind the comedy.
Miss Mowcher is described with an almost invasive physical specificity — throat she had none, waist she had none, legs she had none worth mentioning.
The comic catalogue runs through every part of her body as though cataloguing a deficiency.
And she exists — at least in this introduction — entirely to serve Steerforth's vanity, ogling him, catering to him.
The novel will complicate her later — she earns her dignity — but here she is framed by the powerful young man's drawing room.
Even comedy in Dickens encodes a social position.
I wonder if we might also pause over Aunt Betsey's great confession — the passage about her lost investments — because it shows a quite different register of the novel's comedy.
It is comedy in the service of genuine pathos — which is Dickens at his most characteristic.
She recounts her financial ruin in the third person — as though speaking of a stranger — which is itself a small masterpiece of self-protection.

"Betsey funded her property for some time, and then, by the advice of her man of business, laid it out on landed security. That did very well, and returned very good interest, till Betsey was paid off. I am talking of Betsey as if she was a man-of-war."

"So she took her pigs to a foreign market; and a very bad market it turned out to be. First, she lost in the mining way, and then she lost in the diving way — fishing up treasure, or some such Tom Tiddler nonsense — and then she lost in the mining way again, and, last of all, to set the thing entirely to rights, she lost in the banking way."
Tom Tiddler nonsense — that one phrase does the work of a whole chapter of financial satire.
And the way she accumulates the losses — mining, then diving, then mining again, then banking — is the rhythm of a woman who will not be defeated by self-pity.
She names the disaster completely, and then she closes it: least said, soonest mended.
That closing line — least said, soonest mended — lands like a door being firmly shut, and it is absolutely perfect for her.
Betsey Trotwood is one of those characters who seems to have a life that extends beyond the pages she appears in.
You believe entirely that she has been to foreign markets, that she has dabbled in mining and diving and banking — and lost the lot with her chin held high.
That is what great comic characterisation does — it makes you trust the character's offstage life completely.
What we've been circling, in all three passages, is the way this novel uses a child's experience of the world to expose what adults do with power — kindly, cruelly, comically.

And that brings us, in our next segment, to the mechanisms by which that power is applied most systematically — the schools, the workplaces, the institutions that grind a boy into shape whether he consents or not.
We've been tracing David's inner life as he grows — that strange, watching self-consciousness at the heart of the novel.
But Dickens doesn't just give us a sensitive child — he gives us a world of institutions designed, it seems, to grind that sensitivity down.
Daniel, you've been looking at the social machinery that operates throughout this novel — the schools, the law courts, the whole apparatus of shame and control.
Yes, and the place to start — really the foundational image of institutional cruelty in this novel — is the placard.
David is made to wear a sign at Salem House that reads 'Take care of him. He bites.'
It reduces a child to a dangerous animal — and the school enforces it with bureaucratic relish.
But what Dickens captures — and this is the psychological genius of the passage — is not just the humiliation, but what it does to the child's mind.
Listen to this — Dickens writes it in the first person, which makes it all the more devastating:
'What I suffered from that placard, nobody can imagine. Whether it was possible for people to see me or not, I always fancied that somebody was reading it.'
The surveillance has been internalised. He doesn't need the gatekeeper watching him — he watches himself.
And then the text does something extraordinary — David begins to believe he actually is the wild boy the placard describes.
That internalisation is real, and it speaks to the lasting damage cruelty inflicts on an impressionable character.
But I'd resist the temptation to treat the gatekeeper and his wooden leg as representatives of some systematic apparatus.
He is a petty tyrant — as petty tyrants have existed in every age and every arrangement of society.
What matters morally — what Dickens cares about — is the individual cruelty of Murdstone, of the gatekeeper, of Miss Murdstone with her steel purse and her cold will.
Speaking of Miss Murdstone — there is a scene where she refuses even the mildest comparison between David and Murdstone's infant, and it reveals the depth of her territorial malice.
She declares — and Dickens gives her magnificent comic venom here —
'They are not at all alike. They are exactly unlike. They are utterly dissimilar in all respects. I hope they will ever remain so.'
Three parallel negations — and then that final spite: I hope they will ever remain so.
Edmund is right that Dickens loves his monsters as individuals — each one precisely calibrated.
Miss Murdstone's speech is a masterclass in how comic repetition becomes something genuinely sinister.
When you perform that passage aloud, you feel the rhythm tighten with each sentence — 'not at all alike,' 'exactly unlike,' 'utterly dissimilar' — it's like watching someone screw down a lid.
But Daniel's point about the placard stays with me, because Dickens is doing something there that goes beyond the individual persecutor.
The institution requires the label. The gatekeeper's job is to enforce it.
And what Dickens shows — with that beautiful, horrible detail about the baker and the butcher reading it — is that the whole social world becomes a theatre of humiliation.
And institutions don't need to be visibly brutal to do their damage — sometimes they operate through sheer somnolent indifference.
The Doctors' Commons sequence is Dickens at his most Swiftian — and it's one of the great satirical set-pieces of the novel.
David enters this court expecting the majesty of the law, and finds something closer to a gentlemen's club in light hibernation.
Dickens builds to the perfect verdict, and I want to read the whole sentence because the accumulation of adjectives is the argument:

'Altogether, I have never, on any occasion, made one at such a cosey, dosey, old-fashioned, time-forgotten, sleepy-headed little family-party in all my life; and I felt it would be quite a soothing opiate to belong to it in any character—except perhaps as a suitor.'
That final word — suitor — lands like a blade.
For everyone inside the machine, it is cosy and warm. For the person the machine is supposed to serve, it is something else entirely.
'Cosey, dosey, sleepy-headed' — Dickens is practically singing that sentence.
He knows exactly when to let comedy carry the critique — and here the laughter is the critique.
The judge who looks like an owl in an aviary — you can hear the courtroom sketch, practically music-hall.
And yet — and this is where Dickens never lets you off the hook — Emily's fate is partially decided by institutions like this one.
Emily is, for me, the novel's most searching test of where Dickens's sympathies truly lie.
Her letter — which Ham reads aloud — is a document of total self-condemnation, and Dickens gives her a voice of extraordinary fragmented anguish.
She writes — and this is almost unbearable to read quietly, let alone aloud —
'Oh, if you knew how my heart is torn. If even you, that I have wronged so much, that never can forgive me, could only know what I suffer! I am too wicked to write about myself!'
'Too wicked to write about myself' — the shame has become total self-erasure.
One may deplore the social conditions that magnify her transgression — but Dickens asks us also to take the moral weight of that transgression seriously, on its own terms.
I take the moral weight seriously — but I won't separate it from the social weight.
Emily's second letter — the one Rosa Dartle intercepts, in effect — is, if anything, more devastating.
She writes about the wind — and in Dickens's hands it becomes something almost supernatural:
'Tell him that if I was to die tomorrow (and oh, if I was fit, I would be so glad to die!) I would bless him and uncle with my last words, and pray for his happy home with my last breath!'
That parenthetical — 'oh, if I was fit, I would be so glad to die' — is the most wretched line in the novel.
She doesn't feel she even has the right to wish for death's release, because she is not worthy of it.
That is what shame — socially enforced, institutionally amplified — actually does to a person.
And there is a third image of what the social machinery ultimately produces — the emigrant ship.
When David goes down into the hold, Dickens gives us a kind of secular Judgement Day — every age, every occupation, pressed together in the dark.
The passage is so rich I hardly want to interrupt it with commentary — but here is the great sentence:

'From babies who had but a week or two of life behind them, to crooked old men and women who seemed to have but a week or two of life before them; and from ploughmen bodily carrying out soil of England on their boots, to smiths taking away samples of its soot and smoke upon their skins.'
The ploughmen carry England in their boots. The smiths carry it in their skin.
They are England, departing. And Dickens knows it, and lets the image speak for itself.
The emigrant ship is genuinely one of the great passages of English prose — I will concede that without reservation.
The Micawbers, Mr. Peggotty, Emily — all bound for a new world that Dickens himself is not entirely certain will redeem them.
There is a melancholy to the scene that resists easy resolution — which is precisely where Dickens is at his most honest.
Shame, surveillance, institutions that serve themselves — these are the forces David navigates, and somehow survives.
But there's another force at work in his formation — perhaps the most seductive and the most dangerous: Steerforth.
The charm that corrupts — that's where we go next.
We've been examining how Dickens constructs systems of humiliation — social, institutional, almost architectural.
But there's a subtler form of corruption in this novel — one that wears the face of charm.
I want to turn now to the emotional heart of David's story — the people he loves, and what that love costs him.
What strikes me, returning to these passages, is how completely Dickens builds his moral argument through memory rather than judgment.
David doesn't lecture us about loyalty or devotion — he simply remembers Peggotty.
And there's a passage where that memory becomes almost unbearable in its precision.

"Peggotty was the best, the truest, the most faithful, most devoted, and most self-denying friend and servant in the world; who had ever loved me dearly, who had ever loved my mother dearly; who had held my mother's dying head upon her arm."
The accumulation of superlatives isn't sentimentality — it's a boy's desperate testimony.
And then the sentence breaks down entirely — he cannot finish it.
He says, quite plainly, 'I broke down' — twice — as if repetition is the only honest response to grief.
Edmund puts his finger on something that I find extraordinary as a performer — the syntax itself collapses.
Dickens writes 'I broke down, I say' — that 'I say' is not literary padding, it's David catching his breath mid-sentence.
It's a stage direction buried in the prose.
Now contrast that with what happens at the Peggotty boat-house, when David and Steerforth walk in on that extraordinary domestic scene.
The light, the warmth, Ham holding Em'ly's hand, Mr. Peggotty's arms flung open — it's practically a nativity.
And Dickens gives us the key detail in the most droll possible way.
"A clapping of hands: which latter noise, I was surprised to see, proceeded from the generally disconsolate Mrs. Gummidge."
Mrs. Gummidge — clapping like a madwoman — is the thermometer of how happy this moment truly is.
And Steerforth is standing in the middle of it, taking notes.
That image — Steerforth standing in that room — is one of the most chilling in the novel, if you understand what it represents.
Here is a world of genuine, unguarded human feeling — joy, family, belonging — and Dickens frames it as something that can be taken.
Steerforth looks at these people and sees neither their dignity nor their love — he sees their vulnerability.
The class dimension matters enormously here.
Steerforth's charm is a weapon that only functions in one direction — downward.
He cannot corrupt his equals because he has no access to their hearts — only to those, like David, who have been taught to worship him.
I take Daniel's point about class, but I want to resist making Steerforth into a purely structural villain.
The novel is also a study in the undisciplined heart — and that indictment falls on David himself.
There's a line later in the novel — sitting by the fire, reflecting on his marriage to Dora — that is perhaps the moral centre of the whole book.
"I think of every little trifle between me and Dora, and feel the truth, that trifles make the sum of life."
That is Dickens the moralist at his clearest — and his most unsparing.
The problem was never Steerforth alone — it was David's capacity for enchantment, for idol-worship.
Dickens ends that passage with 'Undisciplined heart, reply!' — a direct address to David's own soul.
'Undisciplined heart, reply!' — you could end a play on that line.
What's remarkable is that David knows this about himself — retrospectively, painfully, completely.
And it connects to that earlier passage where he remembers his youthful love as — how does he put it —
"What an idle time! What an insubstantial, happy, foolish time!"
And then: "Of all the times of mine that Time has in his grip, there is none that in one retrospect I can smile at half so much, and think of half so tenderly."
He capitalises Time — Time as a figure, almost a character — and it gives the whole sentence a weight it wouldn't otherwise have.
The foolishness and the tenderness are inseparable — that's Dickens's great insight about first love, and about David specifically.
I want to come back to that reunion scene — Peggotty crying out to David the moment she recognises him.
Three words, and then they're locked in each other's arms in tears.
"My darling boy!"
Dickens doesn't need more than that — and Steerforth is watching this too.
What the novel asks us to see is that Steerforth looks at love and recognises its value — which is precisely what makes him so dangerous.
He doesn't destroy what he doesn't understand — he destroys exactly what he understands perfectly.
Charm as a form of predatory intelligence — that's a line worth sitting with.
And it raises a question about the novel's other great instrument of power — laughter.
Because Dickens is also one of the funniest writers in the language — and humour in this novel can be tender, but it can also be a way of keeping the truth at arm's length.

segments.title: Comedy and Cruelty: The Art of Dickens's Wit

utterances.text: We've been talking about how charm can operate as a kind of corruption — Steerforth's gift for seduction.
But Dickens doesn't only anatomise power through tragedy — he does it through comedy, too, and sometimes the comedy is the cruelty.
And nowhere is that more gloriously on display than Mr. Creakle.
Dickens gives us this terrifying schoolmaster — fiery face, small deep-set eyes, thick veins in his forehead — and then he delivers the masterstroke.
The passage reads:
"he had no voice, but spoke in a whisper."
All that fury, all that swollen menace — and it comes out in a whisper.
That is comic genius. The tyrant undone by his own instrument.
It is very fine, yes. But I'd resist calling it merely comic.
What Dickens is doing there is something more precise — he is showing us how power deforms even its possessor.
The whisper doesn't diminish Creakle — it concentrates him. It makes his anger stranger and more oppressive.
And the child David registers this with complete clarity — the thick veins, the angry face made more angry by the very effort of whispering.
That is a child learning, very early, to read danger in a face.
And what the boys discover later about Creakle is just as revealing.
In the dormitory, Steerforth tells David exactly who this man is. The passage is wickedly precise:
"he was the sternest and most severe of masters; that he laid about him, right and left, every day of his life, charging in among the boys like a trooper, and slashing away, unmercifully."
And then we're told he was a failed hop-dealer, bankrupt in trade, who took to schooling after making away with his wife's money.
This is the man entrusted with children's education. His authority is entirely fraudulent — purchased with someone else's capital.
Dickens is showing us that institutional cruelty is almost always backstopped by financial failure and bad faith.
And yet — and this is the genius of it — the comedy doesn't let the horror off the hook.
Dickens lets the boys laugh at Creakle — bankrupt hop-dealer, can't even raise his voice — and we laugh with them.
But the laughter doesn't dissolve the threat. We know this man still slashes away unmercifully each morning.
Dickens holds both registers simultaneously — the ridiculous and the genuinely dangerous — without letting either cancel the other.
The context for that dormitory conversation is itself remarkable, isn't it — the scene in which it all happens.
Quite extraordinary, yes. Dickens sets the boys' gossip inside a scene of real atmospheric beauty.
The moonlight falling through the window, painting — that word is exact — a pale window on the floor.
And then Steerforth dips a match into a phosphorus-box and sheds a blue glare over them that is gone directly.
That flash of cold light, present and then instantly gone — it is almost a figure for memory itself.
And David tells us, with characteristic precision, that Steerforth brought this glare specifically to look for something on the board.
That passage knocked me sideways when I first recorded it. Listen to how the adult David describes the feeling:

"A certain mysterious feeling, consequent on the darkness, the secrecy of the revel, and the whisper in which everything was said, steals over me again, and I listen to all they tell me with a vague feeling of solemnity and awe."
Steals over me again. Present tense. The memory hasn't merely been recalled — it's been re-inhabited.
And then — this is the touch I love — David says he feigns to laugh when Traddles pretends to see a ghost.
He is frightened. But he performs bravado for the other boys. It is the comic and the vulnerable braided together perfectly.
There's something else operating in that scene, though. These whispers — everything is whispered.
Earlier, Creakle whispers because his voice is broken. Here, the boys whisper because the institution demands their silence.
The cruelty doesn't disappear at night — it shapes even the children's pleasure, drives their joy underground.
The feast itself — the contraband food, the secret revel — is only possible because the normal order is one of total suppression.
I take the point, though I'd frame it differently. What Dickens captures is something more intimate than a critique of institutions.
He captures the irreducible tenderness of boyhood fellowship — the gladness of being together in the dark.
And then — and this is where Dickens breaks your heart — he pivots to the farewell from David's mother.
David hears her calling from the carrier's cart. He looks out and there she stands at the garden gate, alone.
The passage is almost unbearably still:
"It was cold still weather; and not a hair of her head, nor a fold of her dress, was stirred, as she looked intently at me, holding up her child."
Not a hair. Not a fold. The stillness is almost sculptural. And it is the last time he will see her whole and well.
When I read that passage aloud, I always have to stop afterward. It's a sentence that costs you something.
And what makes it work is that Dickens earns it. We've had the comedy, the Creakle grotesquerie, the midnight feast.
And then, without preparation, this image of absolute stillness and love. The novel knows when to go quiet.
The comedy and the cruelty in this novel are never decorative. They're diagnostic.
Dickens uses laughter to expose the logic of systems — the bankrupt hop-dealer who becomes a schoolmaster, the whispering tyrant.
And then he turns the same lens on the emotional life — David's shame, David's grief, David's recklessness.
That morning-after passage — David waking in disgrace after the drunken evening when Agnes saw him — is almost too raw to read.
Dickens gives us the full inventory of self-reproach:
"the agony of mind, the remorse, and shame I felt when I became conscious next day!"
And then it escalates — offences forgotten, an indelible look from Agnes, the impossibility of going out, or even getting up.
That last detail — can't even get up — is so nakedly true it's almost comic again. Dickens won't let David be noble in his suffering.
And that incapacity — moral, physical, the two thoroughly confused — brings us to what may be Dickens's greatest subject in this novel.
The extraordinary lengths to which David — and so many around him — will go to avoid seeing themselves clearly.
That's where we're headed next — the architecture of self-deception.
We've been enjoying the ways Dickens weaponises comedy — the cruelty hiding inside the laughter.
But there's another layer beneath the wit, and it concerns the stories we tell ourselves — about who we are, what we deserve, and what we feel.
Edmund, I'd like to start with you, because your passages today span the full arc of David's emotional life — from childhood institution to adult confession.
Thank you. What strikes me, returning to these passages, is how Dickens understood that self-deception is not a moral failing so much as a survival mechanism.
The child David, arriving at Salem House, looks at that schoolroom and sees, with absolute clarity, what it truly is.
Dickens gives us the institution stripped of all official pretence — and what remains is devastating.
He writes, and I want to read this carefully:

"Two miserable little white mice, left behind by their owner, are running up and down in a fusty castle made of pasteboard and wire, looking in all the corners with their red eyes for anything to eat."
Pasteboard and wire. A castle that is not a castle. Mice searching for nourishment in a place that offers none.
That is the whole of Salem House in two sentences — and Dickens places it there without a word of explicit condemnation.
What kills me about that passage — and I've read it aloud more times than I can count — is that smell.
Dickens doesn't stop at the visual squalor. He goes for the nose.
He writes of a strange unwholesome smell — and then he lists it: mildewed corduroys, sweet apples wanting air, and rotten books.
"There is a strange unwholesome smell upon the room, like mildewed corduroys, sweet apples wanting air, and rotten books."
Sweet apples wanting air. That's genius. The sweetness is there — but it's dying, sealed up, unable to breathe.
And it's the precise smell of an institution — that particular combination of suppressed life and enforced enclosure.
Every boarding school in England recognised that smell. Every reader who'd been through one went cold.
And yet the children who inhabit that space are expected to emerge from it formed — improved — ready to take their place in society.
The institution presents itself as a site of cultivation. What Dickens shows is a site of attrition.
The caged bird that neither sings nor chirps — that is not incidental detail. That is the programme.
You do not need children who sing. You need children who have been persuaded not to expect anything better than two inches of perch.
But what's interesting is where the novel goes from there — because David doesn't simply escape the logic of self-suppression.
He internalises it. For years, he cannot see what is plainly in front of him — his own feeling for Agnes.
That is precisely the novel's great moral argument, and I think it's worth being precise about what Dickens is doing with it.
David's blindness to Agnes is not stupidity. It is the consequence of an undisciplined heart — a heart that has not yet learned to see truly.
When he finally confronts her — when self-deception is no longer tenable — the language he reaches for is extraordinary in its scrupulousness.
He says:
"I have not suffered quite in vain. You have not taught me quite in vain. There is no alloy of self in what I feel for you."
No alloy of self. That is a man who has, at great cost, learned to distinguish genuine feeling from self-regarding sentiment.
That is what the novel means by the discipline of the heart — and it is earned over six hundred pages of painful experience.
And then Agnes answers him. Five words. Five words that contain the whole second half of the novel.
"I have loved you all my life!"
As an actor you learn to resist the temptation to do too much with a line like that.
Because Dickens has already done everything. The simplicity is the performance.
And then he gives you the image that follows — and it's almost unbearable in its tenderness.
"And Agnes laid her head upon my breast, and wept; and I wept with her, though we were so happy."
Though we were so happy. The paradox lands without explanation. That's Dickens at his most quietly devastating.
I want to hold that joy in view — I don't want to dissolve it — but I also can't leave the Micawbers out of this conversation about self-deception.
Because Micawber is the novel's most sustained portrait of a man whose entire identity is constructed from magnificent, doomed self-belief.
And what's remarkable is that Mrs. Micawber — who has watched this self-belief fail, repeatedly, catastrophically — does not abandon it. She doubles down.
On the deck of the emigrant ship, she urges him to plant his flag on the prow and declare:
"This country I am come to conquer! Have you honours? Have you riches? Have you posts of profitable pecuniary emolument? Let them be brought forward. They are mine!"
Now — is this self-deception, or is it something more interesting? It is performance as survival.
The Micawbers cannot afford to see themselves clearly — because a clear view of their circumstances would mean collapse.
Dickens knows this. And he doesn't judge them for it. He loves them for it — which is a more complicated response than simple sentimentality.
That is fairly put. And there's something else in those passages — Dickens's understanding that human vitality is itself a corrective force.
The Traddles passage — when David visits Gray's Inn and finds it transformed by Sophy and the Devonshire girls — is I think one of the most beautiful things in the novel.
He writes:
"If I had beheld a thousand roses blowing in a top set of chambers, in that withered Gray's Inn, they could not have brightened it half so much."
Withered Gray's Inn. The law — dried up, self-enclosed — and into it comes warmth, tea, children's songs.
The institution that deforms in childhood — Salem House — and the institution that is redeemed in adulthood by human love. It is not an accident that both involve children and cages.
Dickens is not naive about institutions. But he believes love is the only architecture strong enough to outlast them.
The Sultan's family admitted on the roll of attorneys — that image alone is worth the price of the novel.
Dickens can't resist it. He builds this exquisite catalogue — pounce and parchment, red-tape, dusty wafers, ink-jars — and then detonates the whole thing with an Arabian Nights fantasy.
It's saying: love does not merely soften the law. Love makes the law look faintly absurd.
Architecture, institutions, the spaces we inhabit — and the way those spaces either trap us or, occasionally, set us free.
That's precisely where we're headed next — because Dickens doesn't simply use setting as backdrop. He makes it fate.

segments.title: Atmosphere and Accident: How Setting Shapes Fate

utterances.text: We've been exploring how David's inner life distorts and conceals the truth — the architecture of self-deception, as we called it.
But Dickens also uses the physical world itself — objects, spaces, faces — to shape and even determine his characters' fates.
There's a passage I find almost unbearably well-made — David, alone during the school vacation, staring at an old door covered in carved names.
Each name belongs to a boy who will return and read that dreadful placard — 'Take care of him. He bites.'
And Dickens lets David imagine each boy's cruelty with absolute specificity.
"There was one boy — a certain J. Steerforth — who cut his name very deep and very often, who, I conceived, would read it in a rather strong voice, and afterwards pull my hair."
Pull my hair. Not strike him, not humiliate him publicly — pull his hair.
The intimacy of that detail is what makes it so chilling — and so precise as a portrait of a child's dread.
What strikes me is that the door itself becomes a kind of fate register — the names cut into it are already, in a sense, David's future.
Steerforth's name cut very deep and very often — that is not incidental detail.
It is the novel's quiet prediction of the depth of his eventual mark on David's life — and the repetition of the wound.
Dickens understood — as the great moralists always do — that character announces itself before we have the language to read it.
I want to stay on that door for a moment, because it is also an institution — a system of legibility within the school.
The boys who carve deepest are asserting ownership — of the space, of the hierarchy, of the right to judge newcomers.
And David, the placard-wearer, cannot carve his own name — he is written upon, not writing.
He looks at forty-five names and feels collectively condemned — 'sent to Coventry by general acclamation,' as the text has it.
And then Steerforth actually arrives — and the scene is simply miraculous in how quickly it reverses everything.
David is carried before this older boy like a prisoner before a magistrate — that's the word Dickens uses, magistrate.
Steerforth inquires into the particulars of the punishment — and then renders his verdict.
"It was 'a jolly shame.'"
Three words — and David is bound to him ever afterwards.
That is how admiration works in childhood — and Dickens catches it without a gram of sentimentality.
The judicial vocabulary is deliberate and important — carried as before a magistrate, inquired into the particulars.
Steerforth exercises authority without any institutional warrant — purely through force of character and social confidence.
That is both his gift and the precise source of his eventual destruction.
Men who govern by charm alone are ungovernable themselves — and Dickens shows us the seed of that tragedy here, in a schoolyard, in a single adjective.
Edmund is right about the charm — but I'd frame it differently.
Steerforth's power is class power made legible at the level of the schoolyard.
He is 'reputed to be a great scholar' and 'very good-looking' and 'at least half-a-dozen years' David's senior — every marker of dominance stacked in his favour before he speaks a word.
And when he finally does speak, he doesn't argue, he doesn't reason — he pronounces.
'A jolly shame' — and the sentence is passed, in David's favour, because Steerforth wills it so.
Now — if the schoolyard door is the novel's first great omen, then what Dickens does with Uriah Heep in the prison scenes is the dark mirror image of it.
The setting of the Model Prison is supposed to be reformatory — an enlightened institution designed to redeem sinners.
And Heep flourishes there — of course he does — because he was always the system's perfect product.
Listen to what he says to David when they meet there.
"I forgive everybody. It would ill become me to bear malice. I freely forgive you, and I hope you'll curb your passions in future."
And then it turns — magnificently — into something quite extraordinary.
"The best wish I could give you, Mr. Copperfield, and give all of you gentlemen, is, that you could be took up and brought here. I pity all who ain't brought here!"
He pities those who remain free. The inversion is complete — and it is very, very funny, and absolutely terrifying at the same time.
Dickens is being savage about the Model Prison and everything it represents — the Victorian fantasy that you could engineer virtue through controlled environment.
What the system actually produces is Uriah — a man who has learned to perform repentance with absolute fluency.
His 'umbleness has simply found a new institutional container — the same submission, now rewarded with privileges rather than punished by exposure.
And the wish that everyone could be 'took up and brought here' — that is the logic of total surveillance made into charity.
I am in complete agreement with Daniel on the satirical target — which is perhaps a first.
But I would locate the horror not in the institution's class function — rather in what Uriah reveals about the corruption of the moral vocabulary itself.
He has mastered the language of Christian forgiveness — and deployed it as a weapon.
'I freely forgive you' — addressed to the man he has spent years attempting to destroy.
That is not comedy — that is a very serious observation about what happens when the forms of virtue are separated entirely from their substance.
And from the prison we move — at the novel's end — to a room in which two women wear away year after year in an unresolvable grief.
Mrs. Steerforth and Rosa Dartle — and Dickens gives us this scene in the most stripped-back prose.
Present tense, no embellishment, just the fact of what happens and will always happen between these two.
"Rosa, come to me. He is dead!"
And then Rosa by turns caresses her and quarrels with her — fiercely claiming 'I loved him better than you ever did.'
'Thus I leave them; thus I always find them; thus they wear their time away, from year to year.'
That triple 'thus' is not rhetoric — it is a death sentence, passed on two living people.
The setting here is not described — we receive no curtains, no furniture, no weather.
The room exists only as the container of their repetition — and repetition is Dickens's true subject in this closing image.
Rosa loved Steerforth too — with a ferocity that Mrs. Steerforth's maternal possessiveness could not accommodate.
And now they are locked together in a grief that is also a permanent quarrel — unable to separate, unable to agree even on who suffered most.
What Steerforth's death leaves behind is this room — two women whose entire existence is now defined by loss of a man who used them both.
Rosa Dartle was marked by him — literally, scarred by the hammer he threw in childhood.
Mrs. Steerforth shaped him, indulged him, made him into what he was — and now inherits the consequence.
Dickens gives them no resolution, no escape, no arc of recovery — only the room, and the years, and each other.
The door in the playground, the prison cell, the timeless room — Dickens's settings do not merely house the story.
They pass sentence on the characters who inhabit them.
After the break, we'll consider what all of this has finally made of David himself — what kind of education this extraordinary novel has given him, and whether it was enough.
We've been exploring how place and weather conspire against Dickens's characters — but of course, the deepest shaping forces in this novel are human ones.
So let's close by returning to where David's education truly begins — not in a classroom, but in the dark, listening to Steerforth.
There's a scene that I keep coming back to — Dickens gives it almost nothing on the page, and yet it does everything.
The boys are sitting in the dark at Salem House, swapping intelligence about Creakle — who he beats, who he fears.
And then someone asks Steerforth what he would do if Creakle ever laid a hand on him.

"he dipped a match into his phosphorus-box on purpose to shed a glare over his reply, and said he would commence by knocking him down with a blow on the forehead from the seven-and-sixpenny ink-bottle that was always on the mantelpiece"
The phosphorus match — that theatrical glare in the darkness — Dickens gives Steerforth his own lighting rig.
And then: "We sat in the dark for some time, breathless."
That's not just the boys. That's the reader. That's David. That's all of us — breathless before Steerforth.
Oliver has identified something important — the scene is a kind of initiation, isn't it.
The younger boys learn, in the dark, that there is a hierarchy — and that Steerforth sits at the top of it.
But what Dickens is really giving us is the education of David's heart — his capacity for admiration.
It is a faculty that will serve him poorly, and serve him well, in more or less equal measure throughout this novel.
And the passage where David watches Steerforth sleeping in the moonlight captures this with extraordinary tenderness and precision.
"No veiled future dimly glanced upon him in the moonbeams. There was no shadowy picture of his footsteps, in the garden that I dreamed of walking in all night."
Dickens withholds what he knows and what we know — that Steerforth will ruin lives, will end badly.
In its restraint, that passage is as morally serious as anything in the novel.
I want to sit with what's also happening in that dormitory gossip session — because it's not only about Steerforth.
Listen to what else David hears in the dark — the school's entire economy laid bare.
"I heard that one boy, who was a coal-merchant's son, came as a set-off against the coal-bill, and was called, on that account, 'Exchange or Barter'"
A child named after an accounting transaction. That is not a joke — or rather, it is a joke, and it is also the truth of what this institution does.
Children are commodities at Salem House. Parents pay in goods or labour, and the school's power rests on that dependency.
And then — in the same breath — we learn that Mr. Mell "hadn't a sixpence to bless himself with" and that his mother is as poor as Job.
David knows something that implicates Steerforth — knows about the breakfast, hears the echo of "My Charley" — and he stays silent.
That silence is the beginning of David's moral education — and the first small cost of loving Steerforth.
Daniel has put his finger on it — David's gladness at his own silence is one of the novel's most quietly devastating moments.
He says — the adult David, looking back — "I was, I am glad to remember, as mute as a mouse about it."
That "I am glad to remember" is doing enormous work — the present tense breaking through into the past.
He's reassuring himself — even now, even as a grown man — that he did the decent thing.
Which means the guilt is still live. The wound hasn't closed. Dickens is extraordinary at that.
And this is where the moonlight passage becomes so resonant in retrospect.
David raises himself in bed to look at Steerforth — this boy who is already exerting a kind of gravitational pull on his soul.
"He was a person of great power in my eyes" — David says it plainly, without defence.
And Dickens lets the moonlight fall on Steerforth without prophecy, without warning — because that is precisely how enchantment works.
We are not given the wisdom to see the danger in what we love. That is the human condition, not a flaw in David's character.
I'd only add that the novel is clear-eyed about what Steerforth's power is made of — it is the power of class, of ease, of never being struck.
Creakle beats every boy but Steerforth. That is not charm — that is social immunity, and David absorbs the lesson without knowing he's learning it.
What this novel does — and it does it with devastating consistency — is show us how a sensitive, decent person can be educated into deference.
David's education at Salem House is not in Latin or arithmetic. It's in who counts and who doesn't.
And Dickens makes it irresistible — that's his genius and his danger as a novelist.
We sit in the dark with David, breathless before Steerforth's phosphorus match — and we find him magnificent too.
The novel asks us to feel what David feels — so that when the reckoning comes, it lands on us as well.
That feels like the right place to bring this conversation to a close.
We began in darkness — the darkness of Creakle's school, of Steerforth's phosphorus glare — and we end in moonlight, with David watching the boy he cannot yet read clearly.
It's a novel that earns its great emotional weight through exactly these small, precise, devastating details.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, whose ear for Dickens's comic timing remains, as ever, matchless.
To Sir Edmund Leigh, who kept us honest about the moral seriousness at the novel's core.
And to Dr. Daniel Rosen, who ensured we never forgot what the school, the institution, the system actually costs the people inside it.
And to you, for listening — for sitting with us, as David sat with Steerforth, in the dark.

matters to herself. ‘—I don’t mean your sister, Trot, my
dear, but myself—had a certain property. It don’t matter how much;
enough to live on. More; for she had saved a little, and added to it. Betsey
funded her property for some time, and then, by the advice of her man of
business, laid it out on landed security. That did very well, and returned very
good interest, till Betsey was paid off. I am talking of Betsey as if she was a
man-of-war. Well! Then, Betsey had to look about her, for a new investment. She
thought she was wiser, now, than her man of business, who was not such a good
man of business by this time, as he used to be—I am alluding to your
father, Agnes—and she took it into her head to lay it out for herself. So
she took her pigs,’ said my aunt, ‘to a foreign market; and a very
bad market it turned out to be. First, she lost in the mining way, and then she
lost in the diving way—fishing up treasure, or some such Tom Tiddler
nonsense,’ explained my aunt, rubbing her nose; ‘and then she lost
in the mining way again, and, last of all, to set the thing entirely to rights,
she lost in the banking way. I don’t know what the Bank shares were worth
for a little while,’ said my aunt; ‘cent per cent was the lowest of
it, I believe; but the Bank was at the other end of the world, and tumbled into
space, for what I know; anyhow, it fell to pieces, and never will and never can
pay sixpence; and Betsey’s sixpences were all there, and there’s an
end of them. Least said, soonest mended!’

Mr. Spenlow conducted me through a paved courtyard formed of grave brick
houses, which I inferred, from the Doctors’ names upon the doors, to be
the official abiding-places of the learned advocates of whom Steerforth had
told me; and into a large dull room, not unlike a chapel to my thinking, on the
left hand. The upper part of this room was fenced off from the rest; and there,
on the two sides of a raised platform of the horse-shoe form, sitting on easy
old-fashioned dining-room chairs, were sundry gentlemen in red gowns and grey
wigs, whom I found to be the Doctors aforesaid. Blinking over a little desk
like a pulpit-desk, in the curve of the horse-shoe, was an old gentleman, whom,
if I had seen him in an aviary, I should certainly have taken for an owl, but
who, I learned, was the presiding judge. In the space within the horse-shoe,
lower than these, that is to say, on about the level of the floor, were sundry
other gentlemen, of Mr. Spenlow’s rank, and dressed like him in black
gowns with white fur upon them, sitting at a long green table. Their cravats
were in general stiff, I thought, and their looks haughty; but in this last
respect I presently conceived I had done them an injustice, for when two or
three of them had to rise and answer a question of the presiding dignitary, I
never saw anything more sheepish. The public, represented by a boy with a
comforter, and a shabby-genteel man secretly eating crumbs out of his coat
pockets, was warming itself at a stove in the centre of the Court. The languid
stillness of the place was only broken by the chirping of this fire and by the
voice of one of the Doctors, who was wandering slowly through a perfect library
of evidence, and stopping to put up, from time to time, at little roadside inns
of argument on the journey. Altogether, I have never, on any occasion, made one
at such a cosey, dosey, old-fashioned, time-forgotten, sleepy-headed little
family-party in all my life; and I felt it would be quite a soothing opiate to
belong to it in any character—except perhaps as a suitor.

between me and Dora, and feel the truth, that trifles make the sum of life.
Ever rising from the sea of my remembrance, is the image of the dear child as I
knew her first, graced by my young love, and by her own, with every fascination
wherein such love is rich. Would it, indeed, have been better if we had loved
each other as a boy and a girl, and forgotten it? Undisciplined heart, reply!
c55:p52.summary: David sits by the fire reflecting on the secret dissatisfactions he harbored during his marriage and how he now recognizes the profound value of even trivial moments with Dora.
c55:p52.best_quote: I think of every little trifle between me and Dora, and feel the truth, that trifles make the sum of life.

c35:p110.text:
What an idle time! What an insubstantial, happy, foolish time! Of all the times
of mine that Time has in his grip, there is none that in one retrospect I can
smile at half so much, and think of half so tenderly.
c35:p110.summary: David reflects that of all moments in his life, this idle, foolish time of love is the one he recalls with greatest tenderness.
c35:p110.best_quote: Of all the times of mine that Time has in his grip, there is none that in one retrospect I can smile at half so much, and think of half so tenderly.

c23:p80.text:
She cried, ‘My darling boy!’ and we both burst into tears, and were
locked in one another’s arms.
c23:p80.summary: Peggotty recognizes David and cries out in joy, and they embrace tearfully.

c8:p4.text:
The wooden-legged man turned me about so as to exhibit the placard; and having
afforded time for a full survey of it, turned me about again, with my face to
Mr. Creakle, and posted himself at Mr. Creakle’s side. Mr.
Creakle’s face was fiery, and his eyes were small, and deep in his head;
he had thick veins in his forehead, a little nose, and a large chin. He was
bald on the top of his head; and had some thin wet-looking hair that was just
turning grey, brushed across each temple, so that the two sides interlaced on
his forehead. But the circumstance about him which impressed me most, was, that
he had no voice, but spoke in a whisper. The exertion this cost him, or the
consciousness of talking in that feeble way, made his angry face so much more
angry, and his thick veins so much thicker, when he spoke, that I am not
surprised, on looking back, at this peculiarity striking me as his chief one.
‘Now,’ said Mr. Creakle. ‘What’s the report of this
boy?’
c8:p4.summary: The wooden-legged man displays David's placard; David observes Creakle's fiery face, small eyes, and notably his whispered voice.
c8:p4.best_quote: he had no voice, but spoke in a whisper
characters_present: the man with the wooden leg

c8:p47.text:
I heard all kinds of things about the school and all belonging to it. I heard
that Mr. Creakle had not preferred his claim to being a Tartar without reason;
that he was the sternest and most severe of masters; that he laid about him,
right and left, every day of his life, charging in among the boys like a
trooper, and slashing away, unmercifully. That he knew nothing himself, but the
art of slashing, being more ignorant (J. Steerforth said) than the lowest boy
in the school; that he had been, a good many years ago, a small hop-dealer in
the Borough, and had taken to the schooling business after being bankrupt in
hops, and making away with Mrs. Creakle’s money. With a good deal more of
that sort, which I wondered how they knew.
c8:p47.summary: The boys reveal Creakle's vicious character, his prior bankruptcy as a hop dealer, and his misappropriation of Mrs. Creakle's money.
c8:p47.best_quote: he was the sternest and most severe of masters; that he laid about him, right and left, every day of his life, charging in among the boys like a trooper, and slashing away, unmercifully

c8:p46.text:
How well I recollect our sitting there, talking in whispers; or their talking,
and my respectfully listening, I ought rather to say; the moonlight falling a
little way into the room, through the window, painting a pale window on the
floor, and the greater part of us in shadow, except when Steerforth dipped a
match into a phosphorus-box, when he wanted to look for anything on the board,
and shed a blue glare over us that was gone directly! A certain mysterious
feeling, consequent on the darkness, the secrecy of the revel, and the whisper
in which everything was said, steals over me again, and I listen to all they
tell me with a vague feeling of solemnity and awe, which makes me glad that
they are all so near, and frightens me (though I feign to laugh) when Traddles
pretends to see a ghost in the corner.
c8:p46.summary: David evokes the magical atmosphere of the moonlit dormitory feast, the phosphorus-box glare, whispered talk, and his mixture of fascination and fear.
c8:p46.best_quote: A certain mysterious feeling, consequent on the darkness, the secrecy of the revel, and the whisper in which everything was said, steals over me again, and I listen to all they tell me with a vague feeling of solemnity and awe

c10:p156.text:
I was in the carrier’s cart when I heard her calling to me. I looked out,
and she stood at the garden-gate alone, holding her baby up in her arms for me
to see. It was cold still weather; and not a hair of her head, nor a fold of
her dress, was stirred, as she looked intently at me, holding up her child.
c10:p156.summary: David's mother stands at the garden gate holding the baby up for him to see one last time as he departs.
c10:p156.best_quote: It was cold still weather; and not a hair of her head, nor a fold of her dress, was stirred, as she looked intently at me, holding up her child.

c26:p50.text:
But the agony of mind, the remorse, and shame I felt when I became conscious
next day! My horror of having committed a thousand offences I had forgotten,
and which nothing could ever expiate—my recollection of that indelible
look which Agnes had given me—the torturing impossibility of
communicating with her, not knowing, Beast that I was, how she came to be in
London, or where she stayed—my disgust of the very sight of the room
where the revel had been held—my racking head—the smell of smoke,
the sight of glasses, the impossibility of going out, or even getting up! Oh,
what a day it was!
c26:p50.summary: David awakens to profound remorse for his drunken behavior, horror at offenses forgotten, and unbearable recollection of Agnes's indelible look of regret and wonder.
c26:p50.best_quote: But the agony of mind, the remorse, and shame I felt when I became conscious next day! My horror of having committed a thousand offences I had forgotten, and which nothing could ever expiate—my recollection of that indelible look which Agnes had given me—the torturing impossibility of communicating with her, not knowing, Beast that I was, how she came to be in London, or where she stayed—my disgust of the very sight of the room where the revel had been held—my racking head—the smell of smoke, the sight of glasses, the impossibility of going out, or even getting up! Oh, what a day it was!

c7:p130.text:
I gazed upon the schoolroom into which he took me, as the most forlorn and
desolate place I had ever seen. I see it now. A long room with three long rows
of desks, and six of forms, and bristling all round with pegs for hats and
slates. Scraps of old copy-books and exercises litter the dirty floor. Some
silkworms’ houses, made of the same materials, are scattered over the
desks. Two miserable little white mice, left behind by their owner, are running
up and down in a fusty castle made of pasteboard and wire, looking in all the
corners with their red eyes for anything to eat. A bird, in a cage very little
bigger than himself, makes a mournful rattle now and then in hopping on his
perch, two inches high, or dropping from it; but neither sings nor chirps.
There is a strange unwholesome smell upon the room, like mildewed corduroys,
sweet apples wanting air, and rotten books. There could not well be more ink
splashed about it, if it had been roofless from its first construction, and the
skies had rained, snowed, hailed, and blown ink through the varying seasons of
the year.
c7:p130.summary: David gazes upon the desolate schoolroom, describing its long desks, pegs, scattered exercises, silkworms' houses, trapped mice, a caged bird, and the unwholesome smell throughout.
c7:p130.best_quote: A long room with three long rows of desks, and six of forms, and bristling all round with pegs for hats and slates. Scraps of old copy-books and exercises litter the dirty floor. Some silkworms' houses, made of the same materials, are scattered over the desks. Two miserable little white mice, left behind by their owner, are running up and down in a fusty castle made of pasteboard and wire, looking in all the corners with their red eyes for anything to eat.

c64:p52.text:
‘I must say more. I cannot let you leave me so! For Heaven’s sake,
Agnes, let us not mistake each other after all these years, and all that has
come and gone with them! I must speak plainly. If you have any lingering
thought that I could envy the happiness you will confer; that I could not
resign you to a dearer protector, of your own choosing; that I could not, from
my removed place, be a contented witness of your joy; dismiss it, for I
don’t deserve it! I have not suffered quite in vain. You have not taught
me quite in vain. There is no alloy of self in what I feel for you.’
c64:p52.summary: David insists on speaking plainly, declaring that he could never envy Agnes's happiness with another, and that his love for her is selfless and true.
c64:p52.best_quote: I must speak plainly. If you have any lingering thought that I could envy the happiness you will confer; that I could not resign you to a dearer protector, of your own choosing; that I could not, from my removed place, be a contented witness of your joy; dismiss it, for I don't deserve it! I have not suffered quite in vain. You have not taught me quite in vain. There is no alloy of self in what I feel for you.

c64:p72.text: ‘I have loved you all my life!’
c64:p72.summary: Agnes reveals that her secret is her lifelong love for David.
c64:p72.best_quote: I have loved you all my life!

c64:p98.text:
And Agnes laid her head upon my breast, and wept; and I wept with her, though
we were so happy.
c64:p98.summary: Agnes rests her head on David's breast and they weep together, their tears mingling joy and tender sorrow.
c64:p98.best_quote: And Agnes laid her head upon my breast, and wept; and I wept with her, though we were so happy.

c59:p50.text:
‘I think not, Micawber,’ she rejoined. ‘Not fully. My dear
Mr. Copperfield, Mr. Micawber’s is not a common case. Mr. Micawber is
going to a distant country expressly in order that he may be fully understood
and appreciated for the first time. I wish Mr. Micawber to take his stand upon
that vessel’s prow, and firmly say, “This country I am come to
conquer! Have you honours? Have you riches? Have you posts of profitable
pecuniary emolument? Let them be brought forward. They are mine!”’
c59:p50.summary: Mrs. Micawber urges Mr. Micawber to take his stand on the ship's prow and proudly declare himself a conqueror, demanding all opportunities and riches.
c59:p50.best_quote: This country I am come to conquer! Have you honours? Have you riches? Have you posts of profitable pecuniary emolument? Let them be brought forward. They are mine!

c61:p87.text:
Altogether, it was a scene I could not help dwelling on with pleasure, for a
long time after I got back and had wished Traddles good night. If I had beheld
a thousand roses blowing in a top set of chambers, in that withered
Gray’s Inn, they could not have brightened it half so much. The idea of
those Devonshire girls, among the dry law-stationers and the attorneys’
offices; and of the tea and toast, and children’s songs, in that grim
atmosphere of pounce and parchment, red-tape, dusty wafers, ink-jars, brief and
draft paper, law reports, writs, declarations, and bills of costs; seemed
almost as pleasantly fanciful as if I had dreamed that the Sultan’s
famous family had been admitted on the roll of attorneys, and had brought the
talking bird, the singing tree, and the golden water into Gray’s Inn
Hall. Somehow, I found that I had taken leave of Traddles for the night, and
come back to the coffee-house, with a great change in my despondency about him.
I began to think he would get on, in spite of all the many orders of chief
waiters in England.
c61:p87.summary: David reflects that the Crewler girls and Sophy have transformed Gray's Inn with warmth and life, as if a thousand roses had bloomed there; the contrast between the girls' vitality and the dry legalistic atmosphere is so great it seems like a fanciful dream of the Sultan's court appearing among attorneys.
c61:p87.best_quote: If I had beheld a thousand roses blowing in a top set of chambers, in that withered Gray's Inn, they could not have brightened it half so much. The idea of those Devonshire girls, among the dry law-stationers and the attorneys' offices; and of the tea and toast, and children's songs, in that grim atmosphere of pounce and parchment, red-tape, dusty wafers, ink-jars, brief and draft paper, law reports, writs, declarations, and bills of costs; seemed almost as pleasantly fanciful as if I had dreamed that the Sultan's famous family had been admitted on the roll of attorneys, and had brought the talking bird, the singing tree, and the golden water into Gray's Inn Hall.

c7:p140.text:
There was an old door in this playground, on which the boys had a custom of
carving their names. It was completely covered with such inscriptions. In my
dread of the end of the vacation and their coming back, I could not read a
boy’s name, without inquiring in what tone and with what emphasis HE
would read, ‘Take care of him. He bites.’ There was one boy—a
certain J. Steerforth—who cut his name very deep and very often, who, I
conceived, would read it in a rather strong voice, and afterwards pull my hair.
There was another boy, one Tommy Traddles, who I dreaded would make game of it,
and pretend to be dreadfully frightened of me. There was a third, George
Demple, who I fancied would sing it. I have looked, a little shrinking
creature, at that door, until the owners of all the names—there were
five-and-forty of them in the school then, Mr. Mell said—seemed to send
me to Coventry by general acclamation, and to cry out, each in his own way,
‘Take care of him. He bites!’
c7:p140.summary: David dreads how each boy might mock him for the placard; he imagines Steerforth pulling his hair, Traddles making game of him, and Demple singing the message.
c7:p140.best_quote: There was one boy—a certain J. Steerforth—who cut his name very deep and very often, who, I conceived, would read it in a rather strong voice, and afterwards pull my hair.

c8:p29.text:
I was not considered as being formally received into the school, however, until
J. Steerforth arrived. Before this boy, who was reputed to be a great scholar,
and was very good-looking, and at least half-a-dozen years my senior, I was
carried as before a magistrate. He inquired, under a shed in the playground,
into the particulars of my punishment, and was pleased to express his opinion
that it was ‘a jolly shame’; for which I became bound to him ever
afterwards.
c8:p29.summary: The reputed great scholar and handsome James Steerforth arrives; he defends David's punishment as "a jolly shame," winning David's lasting gratitude.

c63:p85.text:
‘But I forgive you, Mr. Copperfield,’ said Uriah, making his
forgiving nature the subject of a most impious and awful parallel, which I
shall not record. ‘I forgive everybody. It would ill become me to bear
malice. I freely forgive you, and I hope you’ll curb your passions in
future. I hope Mr. W. will repent, and Miss W., and all of that sinful lot.
You’ve been visited with affliction, and I hope it may do you good; but
you’d better have come here. Mr. W. had better have come here, and Miss
W. too. The best wish I could give you, Mr. Copperfield, and give all of you
gentlemen, is, that you could be took up and brought here. When I think of my
past follies, and my present state, I am sure it would be best for you. I pity
all who ain’t brought here!’
c63:p85.summary: Uriah forgives David, hopes for the repentance of Micawber and Agnes, and concludes by expressing his fervent wish that all of them—indeed, everyone—be imprisoned and brought to the reformatory system, pitying all who remain free.

I hope Mr. W. will repent, and Miss W., and all of that sinful lot. You've been visited with affliction, and I hope it may do you good; but you'd better have come here. Mr. W. had better have come here, and Miss W. too. The best wish I could give you, Mr. Copperfield, and give all of you gentlemen, is, that you could be took up and brought here. When I think of my past follies, and my present state, I am sure it would be best for you. I pity all who ain't brought here!

c66:p14.text:
Looking fixedly at me, she puts her hand to her forehead, and moans. Suddenly,
she cries, in a terrible voice, ‘Rosa, come to me. He is dead!’
Rosa kneeling at her feet, by turns caresses her, and quarrels with her; now
fiercely telling her, ‘I loved him better than you ever
did!’—now soothing her to sleep on her breast, like a sick child.
Thus I leave them; thus I always find them; thus they wear their time away,
from year to year.
c66:p14.summary: Mrs. Steerforth suddenly cries out that her son is dead; Rosa alternately caresses her and quarrels with her, revealing deep ambivalence, while David reflects that he always finds them thus.
c66:p14.best_quote: 'Rosa, come to me. He is dead!'

c8:p49.text:
But the greatest wonder that I heard of Mr. Creakle was, there being one boy in
the school on whom he never ventured to lay a hand, and that boy being J.
Steerforth. Steerforth himself confirmed this when it was stated, and said that
he should like to begin to see him do it. On being asked by a mild boy (not me)
how he would proceed if he did begin to see him do it, he dipped a match into
his phosphorus-box on purpose to shed a glare over his reply, and said he would
commence by knocking him down with a blow on the forehead from the
seven-and-sixpenny ink-bottle that was always on the mantelpiece. We sat in the
dark for some time, breathless.
c8:p49.summary: The boys reveal that Creakle has never dared strike Steerforth; Steerforth boasts he would retaliate violently if Creakle tried.
c8:p49.best_quote: he dipped a match into his phosphorus-box on purpose to shed a glare over his reply, and said he would commence by knocking him down with a blow on the forehead from the seven-and-sixpenny ink-bottle that was always on the mantelpiece

c8:p58.text:
I thought of him very much after I went to bed, and raised myself, I recollect,
to look at him where he lay in the moonlight, with his handsome face turned up,
and his head reclining easily on his arm. He was a person of great power in my
eyes; that was, of course, the reason of my mind running on him. No veiled
future dimly glanced upon him in the moonbeams. There was no shadowy picture of
his footsteps, in the garden that I dreamed of walking in all night.
c8:p58.summary: David reflects on his contemplation of the sleeping Steerforth, marvelling at the mystery of him and the inability of premonition to foresee his fate.
c8:p58.best_quote: No veiled future dimly glanced upon him in the moonbeams. There was no shadowy picture of his footsteps, in the garden that I dreamed of walking in all night.

c8:p51.text:
I heard that one boy, who was a coal-merchant’s son, came as a set-off
against the coal-bill, and was called, on that account, ‘Exchange or
Barter’—a name selected from the arithmetic book as expressing this
arrangement. I heard that the table beer was a robbery of parents, and the
pudding an imposition. I heard that Miss Creakle was regarded by the school in
general as being in love with Steerforth; and I am sure, as I sat in the dark,
thinking of his nice voice, and his fine face, and his easy manner, and his
curling hair, I thought it very likely. I heard that Mr. Mell was not a bad
sort of fellow, but hadn’t a sixpence to bless himself with; and that
there was no doubt that old Mrs. Mell, his mother, was as poor as job. I
thought of my breakfast then, and what had sounded like ‘My
Charley!’ but I was, I am glad to remember, as mute as a mouse about it.
c8:p51.summary: The boys continue their gossip: a poor boy is traded against his father's bill; the food is overpriced; Miss Creakle admires Steerforth; Mell is poor and his mother is penniless. David notes Mr. Mell's connection to his breakfast and keeps silent.
c8:p51.best_quote: I heard that one boy, who was a coal-merchant's son, came as a set-off against the coal-bill, and was called, on that account, 'Exchange or Barter'
